svg.title: Transport processes
svg.desc: Diffusion: Net movement: gas or dissolved particles move from high to low concentration. Particles move randomly. No respiration energy is needed. Examples: oxygen, carbon dioxide and urea entering blood plasma. At equilibrium, particles still move but there is no net movement. Faster diffusion: Steeper gradient: greater net movement per second. Higher temperature: more kinetic energy. Larger area: more particles cross at once. Thinner barrier: shorter diffusion path. Osmosis: Water moves from a dilute to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane. No respiration energy is needed. Water gain & loss: Dilute outside: water enters. Plant cell becomes turgid. Its wall prevents bursting. Animal cell may swell or burst. Concentrated outside: water leaves. Plant cell becomes flaccid. Severe loss pulls the membrane from the wall: plasmolysis. Animal cell shrinks. Active transport: Particles move low to high concentration, against the gradient, through membrane proteins. Requires energy from respiration, like moving uphill. Diffusion and osmosis move down gradients. Osmosis is water-only. Where it helps: Roots: take up mineral ions even when soil concentration is lower. Gut: absorbs sugars into blood even when blood concentration is higher. Sugars fuel respiration. Many mitochondria support high energy demand. Osmosis practical: Change salt or sugar concentration. Use equal-size potato cylinders. Record initial mass. Control tissue source, size, solution volume, time and temperature. Include distilled water. Blot consistently, reweigh and repeat. Blotting removes surface liquid. Cut safely. Calculate & interpret: % change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100 2.50 g to 2.20 g: −0.30 ÷ 2.50 × 100 = −12%. Plot concentration on x and mean percentage change on y. The 0% crossing means no net water movement. Positive: gain. Negative: loss. Rate = change ÷ time 0.12 g ÷ 30 min = 0.004 g/min. Investigate anomalies. Repeat near the 0% crossing.
